cassava__mosaic_disease.name: Mosaic disease
cassava__mosaic_disease.summary: A virus that makes cassava leaves twisted and patchy yellow-green, and can greatly reduce your root harvest.
symptoms: Leaves have a yellow and green mosaic pattern
Leaves are twisted, curled or smaller than normal
Plants are stunted and produce fewer, smaller roots
cassava__mosaic_disease.cause: Cassava mosaic viruses (begomoviruses). They spread through infected stem cuttings and are carried from plant to plant by whiteflies.

cultural: Pull out and destroy infected plants early, especially young ones
Do not take cuttings from plants with symptoms
Keep the field free of weeds that host whiteflies
organic: There is no cure for infected plants; removing them is the main control

prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties recommended in your area
Use clean cuttings from healthy plants or certified sources
Plant early in the rainy season so plants grow strong before whiteflies build up
Check fields often in the first 3 months and remove sick plants
cassava__mosaic_disease.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if many plants show symptoms, or to find certified clean planting material and resistant varieties.

cassava__brown_streak_disease.name: Brown streak disease
cassava__brown_streak_disease.summary: A virus that causes yellow patches on leaves and brown, rotten areas inside the roots, making them unfit to eat or sell.
symptoms: Yellow patches or blotches along leaf veins, often on older leaves
Brown streaks or lesions on green stems
Roots have brown, dry, corky rot inside and may be cracked or shrunken
cassava__brown_streak_disease.cause: Cassava brown streak viruses (CBSV and UCBSV). They spread mainly through infected stem cuttings and also by whiteflies.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants as soon as you see symptoms
Harvest early in affected fields to reduce root damage
Never use cuttings from fields that had the disease
organic: There is no cure for infected plants; removing them is the main control

prevention: Plant tolerant varieties recommended by your local research or extension service
Use clean, certified cuttings
Avoid moving cuttings from areas known to have the disease
Check roots of a few plants at harvest to know if the disease is present
cassava__brown_streak_disease.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if many plants show symptoms, or to find certified clean planting material and resistant varieties.

cassava__bacterial_blight.name: Bacterial blight
cassava__bacterial_blight.summary: A bacterial disease that causes leaf spots, wilting and shoot die-back, and spreads easily through cuttings and rain.
symptoms: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown
Leaves wilt, dry and fall off
Sticky gum on stems and shoot tips that die back from the top
cassava__bacterial_blight.cause: The bacterium Xanthomonas phaseoli pv. manihotis (formerly X. axonopodis pv. manihotis). It spreads through infected cuttings, rain splash, tools and people moving through wet fields.

cultural: Remove and burn badly infected plants and plant debris
Avoid working in the field when plants are wet
Clean cutting tools between plants
Rotate with a non-cassava crop for at least one season
organic: No organic spray reliably cures the disease; focus on clean material and sanitation

prevention: Use cuttings only from healthy fields
Plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available
Intercropping (for example with maize or legumes) can slow spread
cassava__bacterial_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease appears in many plants or you need clean planting material.

cassava__green_mottle.name: Green mottle (green mite damage)
cassava__green_mottle.summary: Tiny green mites suck the leaves, leaving pale yellow speckles and small leaves, mostly in the dry season.
symptoms: Fine pale yellow speckles or mottling on leaves
Young leaves at the shoot tip are small and deformed
In severe cases the shoot tip looks like a bare 'candle stick'
cassava__green_mottle.cause: Feeding by the cassava green mite (Mononychellus tanajoa). Mites spread by wind and on cuttings, and build up during dry weather.

cultural: Plant early so the crop is well established before the dry season
Remove and destroy badly damaged shoot tips
Avoid moving cuttings with mites to new fields
organic: Protect natural enemies such as predatory mites (for example Typhlodromalus aripo) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides

prevention: Plant tolerant varieties, often those with hairy leaves
Use clean cuttings
Keep plants healthy with good spacing and soil fertility
cassava__green_mottle.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if damage is severe across the field, as chemical miticides are rarely advised for cassava.

cassava__healthy.name: Healthy
cassava__healthy.summary: Your cassava looks healthy. Keep up the good work!
prevention: Keep using clean cuttings from healthy plants
Weed regularly, especially in the first 3 months
Walk your field often and remove any plant with twisted or yellow leaves
Plant at the start of the rains for strong growth
cassava__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

maize__gray_leaf_spot.name: Gray leaf spot
maize__gray_leaf_spot.summary: A fungal disease that causes long grey rectangular spots on maize leaves and can lower yield in humid weather.
symptoms: Long, narrow, rectangular grey or tan spots between leaf veins
Spots start on lower leaves and move upward
Leaves may dry out completely in severe cases
maize__gray_leaf_spot.cause: The fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. It survives on maize residue and spreads by wind and rain splash in warm, humid weather.

cultural: Rotate with beans, other legumes or other non-cereal crops
Bury or remove old maize residue after harvest
Avoid planting too densely so air can move
organic: Use well-made compost to keep plants vigorous; no organic spray is known to control it well
chemical: If the disease appears before tasselling on a susceptible variety, a fungicide containing azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin or propiconazole can help
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties
Rotate crops every season
Do not plant maize after maize in the same field
maize__gray_leaf_spot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

maize__common_rust.name: Common rust
maize__common_rust.summary: A fungal disease that makes small reddish-brown powdery bumps on maize leaves.
symptoms: Small, raised, reddish-brown pustules on both sides of leaves
Pustules release rusty powder when rubbed
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and dry early
maize__common_rust.cause: The fungus Puccinia sorghi. Spores are carried by wind, and the disease favours cool, moist weather.

cultural: Remove volunteer maize plants
Plant at the recommended time for your area
Keep plants well fed so they tolerate infection
organic: No organic spray is known to give reliable control; use resistant varieties
chemical: On susceptible varieties with early, heavy infection, a fungicide containing mancozeb, azoxystrobin or a triazole such as propiconazole can be used
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant rust-resistant varieties
Avoid very late planting
Check leaves weekly from knee height to tasselling
maize__common_rust.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

maize__northern_leaf_blight.name: Northern leaf blight
maize__northern_leaf_blight.summary: A fungal disease that causes long cigar-shaped grey-green spots on maize leaves and can cut yield badly.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan spots on leaves
Spots often start on lower leaves
Whole leaves may dry out and look burnt
maize__northern_leaf_blight.cause: The fungus Exserohilum turcicum. It survives on maize residue and spreads by wind and rain in moderate, humid weather.

cultural: Rotate with non-cereal crops such as beans
Bury or remove infected residue after harvest
Use recommended plant spacing
organic: No organic spray is known to give reliable control; use resistant varieties and rotation
chemical: If disease appears before tasselling, a fungicide containing azoxystrobin, propiconazole or mancozeb can be used
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Do not plant maize after maize
Check fields regularly in wet weather
maize__northern_leaf_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

maize__healthy.name: Healthy
maize__healthy.summary: Your maize looks healthy. Well done!
prevention: Rotate maize with beans or other legumes
Weed early and keep fields clean
Apply fertiliser or manure as recommended
Check for fall armyworm and leaf spots every week
maize__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

tea__algal_leaf_spot.name: Algal leaf spot
tea__algal_leaf_spot.summary: An alga that makes rough, orange-grey round spots on tea leaves, usually on weak or shaded bushes.
symptoms: Round, raised, velvety spots on the upper leaf surface
Spots are grey-green at first, then orange-brown
Mostly on older leaves of weak bushes
tea__algal_leaf_spot.cause: The parasitic alga Cephaleuros virescens. It spreads by rain splash in warm, wet weather and attacks stressed bushes.

cultural: Prune to improve air flow and light
Improve drainage and soil fertility to make bushes stronger
Remove and destroy heavily spotted leaves
organic: Copper-based sprays that are approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A copper fungicide such as copper oxychloride or copper hydroxide can be used on badly affected bushes
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep bushes vigorous with good nutrition
Avoid too much shade
Make sure water does not stand in the field
tea__algal_leaf_spot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tea__anthracnose.name: Anthracnose
tea__anthracnose.summary: A fungal disease that causes brown dead patches on tea leaves, often starting from the leaf edge or tip.
symptoms: Brown to dark patches on leaves, often from edges or tips
Patches may have a yellow border
Small black dots appear on old patches
tea__anthracnose.cause: Fungi such as Colletotrichum species. They spread by rain splash and enter through wounds, especially in wet weather.

cultural: Pick and remove infected leaves
Avoid wounding leaves during plucking
Prune to improve air movement
organic: Maintain healthy bushes with compost and balanced nutrition
chemical: A copper fungicide, or another fungicide registered for tea in your country, can be used in wet periods
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Use balanced fertiliser; too much nitrogen can increase disease
Keep plucking tools clean
Remove fallen infected leaves
tea__anthracnose.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tea__bird_eye_spot.name: Bird's eye spot
tea__bird_eye_spot.summary: A fungal disease that makes small round spots with a pale centre and dark edge on tea leaves.
symptoms: Small round spots with a grey-white centre and reddish-brown edge
Spots look like a bird's eye
Many spots can make leaves yellow and fall
tea__bird_eye_spot.cause: The fungus Cercospora theae. It spreads by rain splash and wind in wet weather.

cultural: Remove and destroy spotted leaves
Prune to open up the bush
Improve drainage
organic: Keep bushes strong with good nutrition
chemical: A copper fungicide can be used if many leaves are affected
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep bushes vigorous
Avoid overcrowding
Clean up fallen leaves
tea__bird_eye_spot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tea__brown_blight.name: Brown blight
tea__brown_blight.summary: A fungal disease that causes large brown patches on mature tea leaves, mostly on stressed bushes.
symptoms: Large, round to irregular brown patches on mature leaves
Patches have rings and small black dots
Affected leaves may drop early
tea__brown_blight.cause: The fungus Colletotrichum camelliae (Glomerella cingulata). It spreads by rain splash and attacks bushes weakened by stress or wounds.

cultural: Remove infected leaves and prunings from the field
Avoid damaging leaves during plucking
Improve soil fertility and drainage
organic: Strengthen bushes with compost and mulch
chemical: A copper fungicide can be used in severe cases
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep bushes healthy and well fed
Avoid water stress
Clean up fallen leaves
tea__brown_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tea__gray_blight.name: Grey blight
tea__gray_blight.summary: A fungal disease that makes grey-brown patches with dark rings on older tea leaves.
symptoms: Brown patches on leaves that turn grey in the middle
Dark rings or bands around the patches
Small black dots on the grey area
tea__gray_blight.cause: Fungi such as Pestalotiopsis species. They enter through wounds and spread by rain splash in wet weather.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected leaves
Avoid wounding bushes during plucking and pruning
Prune to improve air flow
organic: Keep bushes strong with balanced nutrition and mulch
chemical: A copper fungicide, or another fungicide registered for tea, can be used in severe outbreaks
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep bushes vigorous
Handle bushes carefully to avoid wounds
Remove prunings and fallen leaves
tea__gray_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tea__red_leaf_spot.name: Red leaf spot
tea__red_leaf_spot.summary: Red or reddish-brown spots on tea leaves, usually a fungal leaf spot that worsens on weak bushes.
symptoms: Small red to reddish-brown spots on leaves
Spots may join to form larger patches
Affected leaves may yellow and fall
tea__red_leaf_spot.cause: Usually a fungal leaf spot that spreads by rain splash; the exact fungus can vary, and stress such as poor nutrition makes it worse.

cultural: Remove spotted leaves
Prune to improve air movement
Improve soil fertility and drainage
organic: Use compost and mulch to keep bushes strong
chemical: If spots spread widely, a copper fungicide can be used
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Feed bushes with balanced fertiliser
Avoid water stress
Clean up fallen leaves
tea__red_leaf_spot.getHelp: Ask an extension officer to confirm the cause before spraying, because several problems can make red spots on tea.

tea__white_spot.name: White spot
tea__white_spot.summary: A fungal disease that makes small white or pale spots on young tea leaves and can lower leaf quality.
symptoms: Small white or pale grey spots on young leaves
Spots may have a dark or reddish edge
Leaves can become rough and distorted
tea__white_spot.cause: A fungal leaf disease that spreads by rain splash in cool, wet weather and attacks young flush.

cultural: Remove and destroy spotted leaves
Prune to improve air flow
Avoid heavy shade
organic: Keep bushes healthy with good nutrition
chemical: A copper fungicide can be used during wet periods if many leaves are affected
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep bushes vigorous
Avoid overcrowding
Remove fallen leaves
tea__white_spot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tea__healthy.name: Healthy
tea__healthy.summary: Your tea leaves look healthy. Keep it up!
prevention: Pluck regularly and carefully to avoid wounding bushes
Feed bushes with balanced fertiliser or compost
Prune on time to keep bushes open
Keep drains clear so water does not stand
tea__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

coffee__leaf_rust.name: Leaf rust
coffee__leaf_rust.summary: A fungal disease that makes orange powdery spots under coffee leaves and causes them to fall, weakening the tree.
symptoms: Yellow spots on the upper side of leaves
Orange-yellow powder on the underside of leaves
Leaves fall early and branches may die back
coffee__leaf_rust.cause: The fungus Hemileia vastatrix. Spores spread by wind, rain splash and people, and the disease favours warm, wet weather.

cultural: Prune and stump trees to improve air flow
Remove suckers and keep shade at the right level
Feed trees well so they keep their leaves
organic: Copper-based sprays approved for organic use can be used where allowed
chemical: A copper fungicide (copper hydroxide or copper oxychloride) protects leaves before rust appears
A triazole fungicide such as cyproconazole or triadimefon can be used when rust is already present
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant rust-resistant varieties recommended in your country
Spray protectively at the start of the rains if rust is common in your area
Keep trees vigorous with good nutrition
coffee__leaf_rust.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

coffee__red_spider_mite.name: Red spider mite
coffee__red_spider_mite.summary: Tiny red mites suck coffee leaves, making them look bronze or rusty, mostly in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Upper leaf surface looks dull, bronze or rusty
Very small red mites and fine webbing on the upper side of leaves
Damaged leaves may fall in severe cases
coffee__red_spider_mite.cause: The red coffee mite (Oligonychus coffeae). Mites build up in dry weather and after broad-spectrum insecticides kill their natural enemies.

cultural: Mulch and water where possible to reduce drought stress
Use shade trees to reduce heat stress
Avoid unnecessary insecticide sprays that kill natural enemies
organic: Protect predatory mites and ladybirds by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays
Neem-based products can reduce mite numbers
chemical: Only if damage is severe, use an acaricide registered for coffee, such as sulphur or abamectin where approved
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep trees well watered and mulched in the dry season
Check leaves with a hand lens in dry weather
Keep natural enemies alive
coffee__red_spider_mite.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if mites spread over many trees despite mulching and care.

coffee__healthy.name: Healthy
coffee__healthy.summary: Your coffee leaves look healthy. Great job!
prevention: Prune and remove suckers regularly
Mulch around trees to keep soil moist
Feed trees with manure or fertiliser as recommended
Check leaves for rust and pests at the start of the rains
coffee__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

cashew__anthracnose.name: Anthracnose
cashew__anthracnose.summary: A fungal disease that causes dark spots on young cashew leaves, flowers and nuts in wet weather.
symptoms: Dark brown, water-soaked spots on young leaves and shoots
Flowers and young nuts turn black and drop
Shoot tips may die back
cashew__anthracnose.cause: The fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. It spreads by rain splash and wind during wet, humid weather.

cultural: Prune dead and infected branches and burn them
Space trees well and open the canopy
Remove fallen infected nuts and leaves
organic: Copper-based sprays approved for organic use can be used where allowed
chemical: A copper fungicide or mancozeb can be sprayed at new flush and flowering in wet weather
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Prune trees each year to improve air flow
Keep the orchard clean of fallen material
Use planting material from healthy trees
cashew__anthracnose.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

cashew__gummosis.name: Gummosis
cashew__gummosis.summary: A fungal disease that makes cashew trunks and branches ooze gum and can slowly kill the tree.
symptoms: Sticky gum oozes from cracks in the trunk or branches
Bark under the gum is dark and dead
Leaves yellow and branches die back
cashew__gummosis.cause: The fungus Lasiodiplodia theobromae. It enters through wounds and attacks trees under stress.

cultural: Scrape away dead bark and gum down to healthy wood
Burn the scraped material
Avoid wounding trunks with tools or fire
organic: Cover scraped wounds with a Bordeaux paste (copper sulphate and lime) where allowed
chemical: After scraping, paint the wound with a copper fungicide paste
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Avoid injuring trees
Keep trees healthy with good spacing and care
Remove dead branches regularly
cashew__gummosis.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if many trees are oozing gum or trees are dying.

cashew__leaf_miner.name: Leaf miner
cashew__leaf_miner.summary: A small moth larva tunnels inside young cashew leaves, leaving pale blisters and curled leaves.
symptoms: Silvery or pale blister-like patches on young leaves
Leaves curl, dry and may fall
Damage is worst on new flush
cashew__leaf_miner.cause: Larvae of the cashew leaf miner moth (Acrocercops syngramma), which lays eggs on young, tender leaves.

cultural: Remove and destroy badly mined young leaves
Prune to encourage even flushing
Protect natural enemies such as wasps and ants
organic: Neem-based sprays on new flush can reduce damage
chemical: If damage is heavy on new flush, use an insecticide registered for cashew, such as lambda-cyhalothrin
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Check new flush every week
Act early when new leaves appear
Avoid unnecessary sprays that kill natural enemies
cashew__leaf_miner.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if most new leaves are damaged each flush.

cashew__red_rust.name: Red rust
cashew__red_rust.summary: An alga that makes rusty orange-red patches on cashew leaves, mostly on old or shaded leaves.
symptoms: Round, raised, rust-coloured patches on leaves
Patches feel velvety
Mostly on older leaves in the lower canopy
cashew__red_rust.cause: The parasitic alga Cephaleuros species. It spreads by rain splash in warm, wet weather.

cultural: Prune to open the canopy and let in light
Remove heavily affected leaves
Improve tree nutrition
organic: Copper-based sprays approved for organic use can be used where allowed
chemical: A copper fungicide such as copper oxychloride can be used if many leaves are affected
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Prune trees each year
Avoid overcrowding
Keep trees well fed
cashew__red_rust.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

cashew__healthy.name: Healthy
cashew__healthy.summary: Your cashew leaves look healthy. Keep it up!
prevention: Prune trees each year to keep the canopy open
Clear weeds and dry grass to prevent bush fires
Check new flush for pests every week
Remove fallen diseased nuts and leaves
cashew__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

apple__scab.name: Apple scab
apple__scab.summary: A fungal disease that makes dark scabby spots on apple leaves and fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves
Dark, cracked, scabby spots on fruit
Leaves may yellow and fall early
apple__scab.cause: The fungus Venturia inaequalis. It survives in fallen leaves and spreads by rain splash and wind in cool, wet weather.

cultural: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves
Prune to open the tree canopy
Remove badly infected fruit
organic: Sulphur sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A protectant fungicide such as captan or mancozeb from bud break in wet weather
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant scab-resistant varieties
Keep the orchard floor clean
Prune each year for good air flow
apple__scab.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

apple__black_rot.name: Black rot
apple__black_rot.summary: A fungal disease that causes purple-edged leaf spots, rotting fruit and cankers on apple branches.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves that become brown with a purple edge
Fruit rot that turns black, often starting at the blossom end
Sunken cankers on branches
apple__black_rot.cause: The fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It survives in dead wood, cankers and dried fruit, and spreads by rain splash.

cultural: Prune out dead wood and cankers and burn them
Remove dried, shrivelled fruit from trees and ground
Avoid wounding trees
organic: Copper or sulphur sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A protectant fungicide such as captan during wet weather
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep trees healthy and free of dead wood
Clean up fallen fruit
Prune each year
apple__black_rot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

apple__cedar_apple_rust.name: Cedar apple rust
apple__cedar_apple_rust.summary: A fungal disease that makes bright orange spots on apple leaves; it needs juniper (cedar) trees nearby to survive.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper side of leaves
Small tube-like growths under the spots
Leaves may fall early
apple__cedar_apple_rust.cause: The fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It alternates between juniper (cedar) trees and apple, and spreads by wind in wet spring weather.

cultural: Remove nearby juniper trees if possible
Remove galls from junipers before spring
Rake up fallen apple leaves
organic: Sulphur sprays approved for organic use can give some protection where allowed
chemical: A fungicide such as myclobutanil from pink bud stage in wet weather
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant apple varieties
Avoid planting apples near junipers
apple__cedar_apple_rust.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

apple__healthy.name: Healthy
apple__healthy.summary: Your apple tree looks healthy. Nice work!
prevention: Prune each year to open the canopy
Clean up fallen leaves and fruit
Water during dry spells and mulch the base
Check leaves and fruit regularly for spots
apple__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

blueberry__healthy.name: Healthy
blueberry__healthy.summary: Your blueberry plant looks healthy. Keep it up!
prevention: Keep soil acidic and well mulched
Water regularly, especially when fruiting
Prune old and weak canes
Remove fallen leaves and fruit
blueberry__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

raspberry__healthy.name: Healthy
raspberry__healthy.summary: Your raspberry plant looks healthy. Well done!
prevention: Remove old canes after fruiting
Keep rows narrow for good air flow
Mulch and water regularly
Remove wild brambles nearby that can carry disease
raspberry__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

soybean__healthy.name: Healthy
soybean__healthy.summary: Your soybean looks healthy. Good job!
prevention: Rotate soybean with maize or other cereals
Use clean, good-quality seed
Weed early
Check leaves for rust and pests regularly
soybean__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

cherry__powdery_mildew.name: Powdery mildew
cherry__powdery_mildew.summary: A fungal disease that covers cherry leaves with white powder and can curl young leaves.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves and shoots
Young leaves curl or pucker
Fruit may have a light powdery coat
cherry__powdery_mildew.cause: The fungus Podosphaera clandestina. It spreads by wind and favours warm days, humid nights and shaded, crowded trees.

cultural: Prune to improve air flow and light
Remove infected shoots
Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser
organic: Sulphur or potassium bicarbonate sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A fungicide such as myclobutanil or another product registered for cherries
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Prune each year
Do not overcrowd trees
Check young leaves often in warm, humid weather
cherry__powdery_mildew.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

cherry__healthy.name: Healthy
cherry__healthy.summary: Your cherry tree looks healthy. Keep it up!
prevention: Prune each year to keep the canopy open
Water in dry periods and mulch the base
Clean up fallen leaves and fruit
Check for leaf spots and powdery patches
cherry__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

grape__black_rot.name: Black rot
grape__black_rot.summary: A fungal disease that causes brown leaf spots and turns grapes into hard black mummies.
symptoms: Round brown spots with dark edges on leaves
Berries turn brown, then black, hard and shrivelled
Black dots on spots and shrivelled berries
grape__black_rot.cause: The fungus Guignardia bidwellii. It survives in mummified berries and spreads by rain splash in warm, wet weather.

cultural: Remove and destroy mummified berries and infected leaves
Prune for good air flow
Control weeds under vines
organic: Copper or sulphur sprays approved for organic use give some protection where allowed
chemical: A protectant fungicide such as mancozeb or captan from early shoot growth to berry set
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Clean up all mummies before the season
Train and prune vines for an open canopy
Plant in sunny, well-drained sites
grape__black_rot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

grape__esca.name: Esca (black measles)
grape__esca.summary: A long-term wood disease of grapevines that causes striped leaves and spotted berries and can kill vines.
symptoms: Leaves with yellow or red stripes between veins that dry out ('tiger stripes')
Small dark spots on berries
Dark streaks in the wood when cut; vines may suddenly wilt and die
grape__esca.cause: A group of wood-rotting fungi (such as Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium species) that enter through pruning wounds.

cultural: Cut out dead and infected wood well below the damage
Prune in dry weather
Remove and burn badly affected vines
organic: Protect large pruning cuts with a wound sealant

prevention: Use healthy planting material
Make pruning cuts small and in dry weather
Protect pruning wounds
grape__esca.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if many vines show symptoms; there is no spray that cures esca.

grape__leaf_blight.name: Leaf blight (Isariopsis leaf spot)
grape__leaf_blight.summary: A fungal disease that makes dark brown spots on grape leaves and can cause early leaf drop.
symptoms: Irregular dark brown spots on leaves
Spots may join and leaves dry out
Leaves fall early
grape__leaf_blight.cause: The fungus Pseudocercospora vitis (Isariopsis). It spreads by rain splash and wind in warm, humid weather.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected leaves
Prune for good air flow
Clean up fallen leaves
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A protectant fungicide such as mancozeb or a copper fungicide
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Keep the canopy open
Clean up leaves after the season
Avoid overhead watering
grape__leaf_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

grape__healthy.name: Healthy
grape__healthy.summary: Your grapevine looks healthy. Well done!
prevention: Prune each year for an open canopy
Remove old berries and leaves after harvest
Water at the base, not over the leaves
Check leaves and bunches for spots regularly
grape__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

orange__citrus_greening.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
orange__citrus_greening.summary: A serious bacterial disease spread by small insects that makes citrus leaves blotchy yellow and fruit small and bitter. There is no cure.
symptoms: Blotchy, uneven yellowing on leaves (not the same on both sides)
Small, lopsided fruit that stays green and tastes bitter
Branches die back and the tree declines
orange__citrus_greening.cause: Bacteria (Candidatus Liberibacter species) carried by citrus psyllids, including the African citrus psyllid (Trioza erytreae) and the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri), and spread by infected planting material.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected trees to protect healthy ones
Remove psyllid host plants near the orchard
Do not move budwood or seedlings from affected areas
organic: Protect natural enemies of psyllids such as ladybirds and parasitic wasps
chemical: To control psyllids, use an insecticide registered for citrus, such as imidacloprid, especially on new flush
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Buy seedlings only from certified clean nurseries
Check new flush for psyllids regularly
Replant with clean trees after removing sick ones
orange__citrus_greening.getHelp: Contact an extension officer as soon as you suspect greening, so it can be confirmed and neighbours warned.

peach__bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
peach__bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease that causes small dark spots and holes in peach leaves and spots on fruit.
symptoms: Small, angular dark spots on leaves
Spot centres fall out, leaving holes ('shot holes')
Sunken dark spots or cracks on fruit
peach__bacterial_spot.cause: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads by rain splash and wind in warm, wet weather.

cultural: Prune for good air flow
Remove badly infected twigs
Avoid overhead watering
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A copper bactericide such as copper hydroxide, used at low rates to avoid leaf burn
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Keep trees vigorous with balanced fertiliser
Avoid sites exposed to strong, sandy winds
peach__bacterial_spot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

peach__healthy.name: Healthy
peach__healthy.summary: Your peach tree looks healthy. Keep it up!
prevention: Prune each year to open the centre of the tree
Water in dry spells and mulch
Clean up fallen leaves and fruit
Check leaves for spots and curling
peach__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

pepper__bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
pepper__bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease that makes small dark spots on pepper leaves and fruit and causes leaves to fall.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown
Leaves turn yellow and drop
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
pepper__bacterial_spot.cause: Xanthomonas bacteria. They spread through infected seed and seedlings, rain splash, and handling wet plants.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants and debris
Do not work among plants when they are wet
Rotate away from pepper and tomato for 2–3 years
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can slow spread where allowed
chemical: A copper bactericide, sometimes mixed with mancozeb, applied early
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Use clean, certified seed and healthy seedlings
Water at the base, not over leaves
Rotate crops
pepper__bacterial_spot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

pepper__healthy.name: Healthy
pepper__healthy.summary: Your pepper plant looks healthy. Great job!
prevention: Water at the base of the plant
Rotate peppers with non-related crops
Mulch to keep soil off the leaves
Check leaves regularly for spots and pests
pepper__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

potato__early_blight.name: Early blight
potato__early_blight.summary: A fungal disease that makes brown spots with rings on older potato leaves.
symptoms: Brown spots with target-like rings on older leaves
Yellowing around spots
Leaves dry and die from the bottom up
potato__early_blight.cause: The fungus Alternaria solani. It survives on plant debris and spreads by wind and rain, especially on stressed plants.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected leaves and plant debris
Rotate away from potato and tomato for 2–3 years
Keep plants well fed
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A protectant fungicide such as mancozeb or chlorothalonil
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Use certified seed potatoes
Rotate crops
Apply balanced fertiliser to avoid plant stress
potato__early_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

potato__late_blight.name: Late blight
potato__late_blight.summary: A very fast-spreading disease that can destroy a potato field within days in cool, wet weather. Act quickly.
symptoms: Dark, water-soaked patches on leaves that spread fast
White fuzzy growth under leaves in wet weather
Brown rot in tubers
potato__late_blight.cause: The water mould Phytophthora infestans. It spreads by wind and rain in cool, wet weather, and survives in infected tubers.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Earth up (hill) plants well to protect tubers
Cut and remove haulms 2 weeks before harvest in infected fields
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can protect plants before infection where allowed
chemical: A protectant such as mancozeb before disease appears in wet weather
A systemic product such as metalaxyl plus mancozeb or cymoxanil plus mancozeb when disease is present
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Use certified seed potatoes
Destroy volunteer potatoes and cull piles
Spray preventively in cool, wet seasons
potato__late_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer immediately if late blight spreads, as it can destroy whole fields quickly.

potato__healthy.name: Healthy
potato__healthy.summary: Your potato plant looks healthy. Keep it up!
prevention: Use certified seed potatoes
Earth up plants to protect tubers
Rotate potatoes with non-related crops
Check leaves often in cool, wet weather for blight
potato__healthy.getHelp: If you see spots, yellowing, wilting or pests spreading on many plants, take a sample to your extension officer.

squash__powdery_mildew.name: Powdery mildew
squash__powdery_mildew.summary: A fungal disease that covers squash and pumpkin leaves with white powder.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves and stems
Leaves turn yellow, then brown and dry
Fruit may be small or ripen early
squash__powdery_mildew.cause: Fungi such as Podosphaera xanthii. Spores spread by wind, and the disease likes warm, dry days and humid nights.

cultural: Remove badly infected leaves
Space plants well for air flow
Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser
organic: Sulphur or potassium bicarbonate sprays approved for organic use where allowed
A diluted milk spray (about 1 part milk to 9 parts water) may help in early stages
chemical: A fungicide such as sulphur or myclobutanil when spots first appear
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Rotate crops
Check leaves often during warm weather
squash__powdery_mildew.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

strawberry__leaf_scorch.name: Leaf scorch
strawberry__leaf_scorch.summary: A fungal disease that makes small purple spots on strawberry leaves that can join and make leaves look burnt.
symptoms: Small, dark purple spots on leaves
Spots join and leaves turn purple-brown and look scorched
Leaves dry and die
strawberry__leaf_scorch.cause: The fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. It survives on old leaves and spreads by rain splash.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected leaves
Space plants for good air flow
Water at the base, not over the leaves
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A fungicide such as captan registered for strawberries
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Renew beds every few years
Use healthy planting material
strawberry__leaf_scorch.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tomato__bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease that makes small dark spots on tomato leaves and fruit.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves
Leaves turn yellow and fall
Small raised scabby spots on fruit
tomato__bacterial_spot.cause: Xanthomonas bacteria. They spread through infected seed and seedlings, rain splash, and handling wet plants.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants and debris
Avoid working with wet plants
Rotate away from tomato and pepper for 2–3 years
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can slow spread where allowed
chemical: A copper bactericide, sometimes mixed with mancozeb, applied early

Water at the base, not over leaves

tomato__early_blight.name: Early blight
tomato__early_blight.summary: A fungal disease that makes brown spots with rings on older tomato leaves.
symptoms: Brown spots with target-like rings on lower leaves
Yellowing around spots
Dark sunken spots near the stem end of fruit
tomato__early_blight.cause: The fungus Alternaria solani (and related Alternaria species). It survives on debris and spreads by wind and rain splash.

cultural: Remove lower infected leaves
Stake and prune plants for air flow
Rotate away from tomato and potato
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto leaves
chemical: A protectant fungicide such as mancozeb or chlorothalonil

Rotate crops

tomato__late_blight.name: Late blight
tomato__late_blight.summary: A very fast-spreading disease that can destroy tomato plants within days in cool, wet weather. Act quickly.
symptoms: Large dark, greasy-looking patches on leaves and stems
White fuzzy growth under leaves in wet weather
Firm brown patches on fruit
tomato__late_blight.cause: The water mould Phytophthora infestans. It spreads by wind and rain in cool, wet weather, and often comes from nearby potatoes.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Stake and prune for air flow
Do not grow tomatoes next to potatoes
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can protect plants before infection where allowed
chemical: A protectant such as mancozeb or chlorothalonil before disease appears in wet weather
A systemic product such as metalaxyl plus mancozeb or cymoxanil plus mancozeb when disease is present
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available
Water at the base, not over leaves
Spray preventively in cool, wet seasons
tomato__late_blight.getHelp: Contact an extension officer immediately if late blight spreads, as it can destroy whole fields quickly.

tomato__leaf_mold.name: Leaf mould
tomato__leaf_mold.summary: A fungal disease, common in greenhouses, that makes yellow spots on top of tomato leaves and olive mould underneath.
symptoms: Pale yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown velvety mould under leaves
Leaves curl, dry and fall
tomato__leaf_mold.cause: The fungus Passalora fulva (Fulvia fulva). It thrives in high humidity, especially in greenhouses and tunnels.

cultural: Open greenhouse vents to lower humidity
Space and prune plants for air flow
Remove and destroy infected leaves
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A fungicide such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb registered for tomatoes
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Keep greenhouse humidity low
Water in the morning at the base of plants
tomato__leaf_mold.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tomato__septoria_leaf_spot.name: Septoria leaf spot
tomato__septoria_leaf_spot.summary: A fungal disease that makes many small round spots with grey centres on tomato leaves.
symptoms: Many small round spots with grey-white centres and dark edges
Tiny black dots in the centre of spots
Lower leaves yellow and fall first
tomato__septoria_leaf_spot.cause: The fungus Septoria lycopersici. It survives on plant debris and spreads by rain splash and wet hands or tools.

cultural: Remove infected lower leaves
Mulch to stop soil splash
Rotate away from tomatoes for 2–3 years
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A protectant fungicide such as mancozeb or chlorothalonil
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

Water at the base, not over leaves

tomato__spider_mites.name: Spider mites
tomato__spider_mites.summary: Tiny mites suck tomato leaves, making them speckled yellow, with fine webbing in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckles on leaves
Fine webbing under leaves and between stems
Leaves turn bronze, dry and fall
tomato__spider_mites.cause: The two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae). It builds up in hot, dry, dusty conditions and after sprays that kill natural enemies.

cultural: Remove badly infested leaves
Water plants well and reduce dust
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural enemies
organic: Spray the undersides of leaves with water to knock mites off
Neem oil or insecticidal soap sprays
chemical: An acaricide such as abamectin or spiromesifen; alternate products to avoid resistance
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Check undersides of leaves in hot, dry weather
Keep plants well watered
Control weeds that host mites
tomato__spider_mites.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if mites keep coming back after treatment.

tomato__target_spot.name: Target spot
tomato__target_spot.summary: A fungal disease that makes brown spots with rings on tomato leaves and can spread to fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with light centres and target-like rings on leaves
Spots may join and leaves die
Sunken brown spots on fruit
tomato__target_spot.cause: The fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It spreads by wind and rain splash in warm, humid weather.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected leaves and debris
Stake and prune for air flow
Rotate crops
organic: Copper sprays approved for organic use can help where allowed
chemical: A fungicide such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Avoid overhead watering
Remove crop debris after harvest
Do not plant too closely
tomato__target_spot.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if the disease spreads quickly, keeps returning after treatment, or you are unsure which product is approved in your area.

tomato__yellow_leaf_curl_virus.name: Yellow leaf curl virus
tomato__yellow_leaf_curl_virus.summary: A virus spread by whiteflies that makes tomato leaves small, yellow and curled and stops plants from fruiting well. There is no cure.
symptoms: Leaves are small, curled upward and yellow at the edges
Plants are stunted and bushy
Flowers drop and few fruit form
tomato__yellow_leaf_curl_virus.cause: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, spread by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). It does not spread through touch or seed.

cultural: Pull out and destroy infected plants early
Control weeds that host whiteflies
Do not plant new tomatoes next to old infected fields
organic: Yellow sticky traps to catch whiteflies
Neem-based sprays to reduce whiteflies
chemical: To control whiteflies, use an insecticide registered for tomatoes, such as acetamiprid or spirotetramat; alternate products to avoid resistance
Follow the label and local regulations, and wear protective gear when spraying.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Raise seedlings under insect-proof net
Leave a break period with no tomatoes between seasons
tomato__yellow_leaf_curl_virus.getHelp: Contact an extension officer if many plants show symptoms, or to find certified clean planting material and resistant varieties.

tomato__mosaic_virus.name: Mosaic virus
tomato__mosaic_virus.summary: A virus that makes tomato leaves mottled light and dark green and spreads easily on hands and tools. There is no cure.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled pattern on leaves
Leaves are distorted or fern-like
Plants are stunted and fruit may ripen unevenly
tomato__mosaic_virus.cause: Tomato mosaic virus. It spreads by touch, tools, clothing and infected seed, and survives a long time in plant debris.

cultural: Pull out and destroy infected plants
Wash hands with soap and clean tools after handling sick plants
Do not smoke or handle tobacco near plants
organic: There is no cure; focus on removing sick plants and hygiene

prevention: Use certified, clean seed and resistant varieties
Rotate crops and remove old plant debris
Handle healthy plants before sick ones
